explanation: Both: knowledge of meaning is enjoined like study, so the Veda is to be expounded; subject, purpose, relation, qualified person set out for the commentary and then for the Veda itself ('commentary too would want these in the second degree').

Both: dharma and Brahman are the subjects of the two portions; Puruṣārthānuśāsana 'dharma-brahmaṇī vedaika-vedye'; Jaimini's second sūtra gives twofold restriction; fourth sūtra denies perception. Vol 1 p.540 body says 'As Jaimini states in his Purusharthanushasana-sutra' (attributing it to Jaimini), while the new English and Vol 1's embedded English p.541 keep it separate from Jaimini; the NOTE reading animitta/vidyamāna-upalambhana is what Vol 1 prints (l.11393).

Both: dharma does not exist before the rite, is formless afterwards, hence 'adṛṣṭa'; no inferential mark; joy/sorrow as mark is granted but known only through the Veda; so injunction alone is the means.
Both: Brahman, though existent, is known from scripture alone (second adhikaraṇa of Brahma-sūtra 1.1.3, cause of origin etc.); 'nāvedavin manute taṃ bṛhantam'; no form or mark so no other means.

Both: knowledge of dharma/Brahman is the direct purpose; not like 'seven continents'/'king is going'; 'dharmo viśvasya jagataḥ pratiṣṭhā'; dharma restrains/helps the weak 'as from a king'; Vājasaneyaka creation passage (Bṛh. Up. 1.4.14, 'dharma is the kṣatra of the kṣatra'); 'brahmavid āpnoti param', 'brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati'. Vol 1 p.545 cites the Vājasaneyaka text once as Śatapatha 14-4-2-26, a citation difference only.

Both: 'tarati śokam ātmavit'; seeker of both knowledges is qualified, a man of the three classes; woman and śūdra need the knowledge but Veda is forbidden to them (no initiation), they learn dharma/Brahman through Purāṇas.

Both: relation as teaching/taught, producer/produced, benefactor/benefited; listeners to attend; six aṅgas serve the deep Veda; Muṇḍaka 1.1.4 'dve vidye veditavye... parā caivāparā ca', aparā = four Vedas + six aṅgas, parā = that by which the Imperishable is reached; ritual part with aṅgas is lower (dharma a means), Upaniṣads higher (Brahman the supreme end).

Both: Taittirīya 'śīkṣāṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ; varṇaḥ svaraḥ mātrā balaṃ sāma santānaḥ'. Vol 1 prints svara/bala (l.11588, 11601), supporting the new NOTE's reading, not svaka/vala. The Śikṣā verse: new 'śambhumate matāḥ' (63 or 64 letters) vs Vol 1 Sanskrit 'sambhavato matāḥ' (l.11655), no English given; the number 63/64 agrees.
Both: letters = a etc., accents udātta/anudātta/svarita (three, Śikṣā), quantity short/long/pluta ('hrasvo dīrghaḥ pluta').

Both: bala = place and effort ('aṣṭau sthānāni varṇānām'; 'aco'spṛṣṭaṃ yaṇas tv īṣat'); sāma = even delivery without faults (gīti, śīghrī, śiraḥkampī; upāṃśu, daṣṭa, tvarita) and with sweetness (mādhurya, akṣara-vyakti); santāna = saṃhitā, vāyav ā yāhi / indrāgnī āgatam, left to grammar. New cites 'aṣṭau sthānāni' as Śikṣā 11, Vol 1 as 13 (l.11751); reference number only.

New: indraśatru was meant as tatpuruṣa ('slayer of Indra'), which by 'samāsasya' needs the final acute; it was said with the first syllable acute, hence bahuvrīhi 'he whose killer is Indra'. Vol 1's embedded English (l.11795) says the same ('not slayer of Indra but slain by Indra', prior member gives the accent, bahuvrīhi). But Vol 1's own Kannada-based body at l.11731-11735 says the reverse: 'Correctly pronounced, indraśatru should mean he whose slayer is Indra (bahuvrīhi) ... Tvaṣṭṛ mispronounced, shifting the sense to a tatpuruṣa', and l.11812 says the wrong accent made the sense 'the destroyer of Indra'. Vol 1 body is internally at odds (l.11801-11806 agrees with the new). The new English agrees with Vol 1's embedded English and with the Sanskrit logic; the Vol 1 body lines are the ones that clash.

Both: Kalpa = sūtras of Āśvalāyana, Āpastamba etc.; dilemma whether Āśvalāyana follows mantra or Brāhmaṇa order; 'darśapūrṇamāsau tu pūrvaṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ', dīkṣaṇīyā in the Brāhmaṇa; answer: Saṃhitā order is for recitation (brahmayajña, Tai. Ār. 2.10.6), not performance; dāśatayī and 'ricyata iva' (Vol 1 reads anaśnan, supporting the NOTE's anaśnan, not anañjan); whole-recitation order is kept; Āśvalāyana applies mantras by śruti, liṅga etc. New adds the 'vācaḥ stome pāriplavam' example, which Vol 1 lacks (searched 'pāriplava', not found).

Both: no contradiction in Āśvalāyana not following Saṃhitā order; Yajus mantras ('iṣe tvā') already stand in sacrifice order, hence Āpastamba follows it; dīkṣaṇīyā is a modification of darśapūrṇamāsa so Āśvalāyana rightly starts there; Kalpa useful.
Both: objection that Āśvalāyana should give only the ṛks (pra vo vājāḥ), not 'namaḥ pravaktre'; answered by guṇopasaṃhāra-nyāya, applications from any Śākhā; 'like Śikṣā, Kalpa is needed'.

Both: Grammar settles form and meaning via prakṛti/pratyaya; Aindravāyava passage (Tai. Saṃ. 6.4.7.3): speech unanalysed, gods ask Indra, boon of the cup for Indra and Vāyu together, Indra splits it in the middle; agnim īḷe speech like ocean-roar, Indra divides it into prakṛti, pratyaya etc. Vol 1 reading 'for me and Vāyu together' supports the new NOTE.

Both: Vararuci's 'rakṣohāgamalaghvasandehāḥ prayojanam' explained by Patañjali; rakṣā (elision, augment, change), ūha (genders/cases modified), āgama ('ṣaḍaṅgo vedo 'dhyeyo jñeyaś ca'; chief of the aṅgas), lāghava (Bṛhaspati/Indra, divine thousand years, man lives a hundred), sandeha (sthūlapṛṣatī: first-member accent = bahuvrīhi, final acute = karmadhāraya).

Both: list te'surāḥ ... sudevo 'si; asuras' 'helayo helayaḥ', 'mleccha = apaśabda'; duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ (Śikṣā 52, indraśatru); yad adhītam (dry fuel); yas tu prayuṅkte (victory, but harmed by bad words); the knower of words is the one harmed since merit in right forms means demerit in wrong ones; wrong forms many; ignorance is a refuge, objection 'killing a brahmin unknowingly'. Wrong forms of 'gauḥ': new gośetalikā, Vol 1 gopotalikā (l.12195, gavī goṇī the same); a letter-level variant, sense untouched.

Both: avidvāṃsaḥ (not knowing the pluti in return salutation, 'say as to women: here am I', 'lest we be like women'); vibhaktiṃ kurvanti (prayājāḥ savibhaktikāḥ kāryāḥ); yo vā imām (one who orders speech word by word, accent, syllable, letter is fit as priest).

Both: Ṛ. 4.58.3 'catvāri śṛṅgā' read grammatically: four horns = noun, verb, preposition, particle; three feet = three times; two heads = nominal and verbal terminations (supports the new NOTE's reading); seven hands = seven cases; bound in chest, throat, head; vṛṣabha from raining; roravīti from ru; great god entered mortals. Also Ṛ. 1.164.45 'catvāri vāk parimitā padāni' as the alternative.

Both: manīṣiṇaḥ, guhā trīṇi nihitāni neṅgayanti, fourth of speech spoken by men; Ṛ. 10.71.4 'uta tvaḥ paśyan': one seeing does not see, to another she opens her body like a wife to her husband; 'lest speech withhold herself'. Vol 1 l.12437 'This half of the verse refers to the ignorant man' answers the NOTE on ardham (the half-verse).

Both: Ṛ. 10.71.2 'saktum iva titaunā punantaḥ': wise purify speech like grain with a sieve; saktu from sac ('hard to purify', Vol 1 reads sacati, supporting the NOTE) or by transposition from kas; friends know friendships; auspicious mark on their speech.

Both: grammarians are those who understand; Sārasvatī iṣṭi expiation for an āhitāgni who uses a bad form; naming on the tenth day, kṛt-ending not taddhita-ending, grammar needed. New: name 'of two syllables' only (Sanskrit text ends 'dvyakṣaraṃ vā'); Vol 1 embedded English (l.12513): 'of two syllables or four' - the 'four' is absent in the Wikisource text; sense slightly touched, Vol 1 has the fuller reading.

Both: Ṛ. 8.69.12 'sudevo asi varuṇa': seven rivers = seven cases, kākuda = palate; vārttika 'siddhe śabdārthasambandhe'; Nirukta introduced, Nirukta/Naighaṇṭuka-Naigama-Daivata verses (gau... to 'apare/apāra/pāpūraṇa'; jahā ... to 'ulba ṛvīsa'; Agni to Ūrjāhuti earth, Vāyu to Bhaga atmosphere, Sūrya to Devapatnyaḥ sky). Gloss on sūrmī: new 'thick iron image', Vol 1 'stout hollow pillar made of iron' (l.12536); Vol 1 reads 'ulbam ribīsam', supporting the new NOTE's ṛvīsa; end-word of Naighaṇṭuka varies in Vol 1 itself.

Both: nighaṇṭu = list of synonyms, 'ten nighaṇṭus' (Amarasiṃha, Vaijayantī, Halāyudha); Naighaṇṭuka has three chapters (earth/worlds/space/time; man and limbs; qualities of plurality, smallness); nigama = Veda, Yāska's 'there is also a nigama', second portion = fourth chapter; third portion fifth chapter = Daivata.

Both: text of three portions in five chapters is the Nirukta, self-sufficient for word-meaning; Yāska's twelve-chapter explanation from 'samāmnāyaḥ samāmnātaḥ' to 'anubhavaty anubhavati' also called Nirukta; four classes of words, particles with various meanings; 'na' prohibition in speech, both in the Veda: 'nendraṃ devam amaṃsata' (prohibition), 'durmadāso na surāyām' (comparison).

Both: derivations are not baseless, some stated in Brāhmaṇas (āhutīnām āhutitvam; indra; 'yad aprathayat tat pṛthivyai pṛthivītvam'), author will cite Brāhmaṇas; grammar alone does not give all derivations ('tad idaṃ vidyāsthānam vyākaraṇasya kārtsnyam'); Nirukta useful for the Veda's meaning.

Both: 'seven metres each higher by four' (gāyatrī 24, uṣṇih 28); gāyatrī/triṣṭubh/jagatī for brāhmaṇa/rājanya/vaiśya fire-setting (Tai. Brā. 1.1.9.6), distinction needs the text on metre; one who sacrifices or teaches with a mantra whose ṛṣi, metre, deity he does not know goes to a stump, pit or perishes. New adds that gāyatrī etc. are established by the ma-group, ya-group (metrical feet); Vol 1 only says 'technical rules'. Vol 1's embedded English lists six metres (jagatī omitted), a lapse only.

Both: Jyotiṣa's purpose 'yajñakālārthasiddhaye' (Vol 1 reads yajña, supporting the NOTE); injunctions of year (saṃvatsaram etad vrataṃ caret), season (vasante brāhmaṇo 'gnim ādadhīta), month (māsi māsi), fortnight (yaṃ kāmayeta vasīyān), day (ekāṣṭakāyām, phalgunī-pūrṇamāse), time of day, nakṣatra (kṛttikāsu); Vol 1 p.584 also reads 'saṃvatsaram ukhyaṃ bhṛtvā'.

Both: 'chandaḥ pādau tu vedasya... tasmāt sāṅgam adhītyaiva' (Śikṣā 41-42): metre feet, kalpa hands, jyotiṣa eye, nirukta ear, śikṣā nose, grammar mouth/face; reward 'honoured in Brahmaloka' (Vol 1 body) / 'great in heaven' (Vol 1 embedded English), a wording difference; Yājñavalkya 'purāṇa-nyāya-mīmāṃsā-dharmaśāstrāṅga-miśritāḥ' = fourteen seats; Mahābhārata 'itihāsapurāṇābhyāṃ vedaṃ samupabṛṃhayet'.

Both: stories of Hariścandra, Naciketas in Aitareya/Taittirīya/Kāṭhaka branches are explained in the Itihāsas; creation, maintenance, dissolution of the Upaniṣads explained in Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas; 'sargaś ca pratisargaś ca' (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.6.25), five marks.

Both: Nyāya's sixteen categories decide which sense a text bears; both Mīmāṃsās clearly useful; Smṛtis of Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta elaborate Vedic rules (twilight 'tad u ha vā ete brahmavādinaḥ pūrvābhimukhāḥ', five great sacrifices); fourteen seats; four mantras cited by Yāska. New: mantras 'by hundreds of other branches' (śākhāntaraśataiḥ); Vol 1 embedded English (l.13023): 'four verses from another Sakha'. The sense (four verses, taken from another branch) is what Vol 1 supports; 'hundreds' is not in Vol 1.

Both: first mantra 'vidyā ha vai brāhmaṇam ājagāma gopāya mā śevadhiṣ te'smi; asūyakāyānṛjave...' - Vidyā asks the brahmin teacher to guard her as his treasure and not to tell her to the envious, crooked, uncontrolled, ritually irregular; so she may be potent / bear fruit.

Both: second mantra 'ya ātṛṇaty avitathena karṇau... tam manyeta pitaraṃ mātaraṃ ca; tasmai na druhyet'; teacher rule in the first, pupil rule in the second; the worldly sentence is untrue and not a human end, its opposite is the true Vedic sentence. Vol 1 reads 'truth' / 'worldly talk which is untrue', supporting the NOTE's anṛta.

Both: teacher fills the pupil's ears with the Veda, root tṛṇatti used in another sense, causing no pain, bestowing nectar (Veda's meaning, leads to divine birth/release); pupil must regard him as chief father and mother, natural parents not chief; no harm to him. For the dull boy: new 'cannot take even half a ṛk or a ṛk; he makes him take a word or part of a quarter-verse'; Vol 1 'fourth part of a verse, or even the eighth part': same idea, different grading.

Both: third mantra 'adhyāpitā ye guruṃ nādriyante': pupils who do not honour the guru in speech, mind, action are not to be enjoyed/protected by him, so the Veda does not protect them (Vol 1 prints śrutaṃ, supporting the NOTE's śrutam, not kṣutam); quoted as Nirukta 2.4.

Both: fourth mantra 'yam eva vidyāḥ śucim apramattaṃ medhāvinaṃ brahmacaryopapannam... tasmai mā brūyā nidhipāya brahma': teach Vidyā to the pure, careful, intelligent pupil who will not harm; Veda knowledge to be taught to the chief pupil; closing colophon of the introduction to the commentary.
